Press Release:


Listeriosis
South Africa is in the grips of a deadly Listeriosis outbreak and with 61 confirmed deaths and over 700 recorded
cases of infection, it’s one of the worst outbreaks the country has ever experienced. From fresh fruit and vegetables
to meat produce, the listeria bacterium can contaminate almost any food items, infecting pregnant women,
vulnerable newborns and the elderly. As the number of infections continues to increase, can the Department of
Health contain this dangerous bacterium?

Script:


LISTERIOSIS


V/O: Listeriosis - named after Joseph Lister - the British pioneer of sterile surgery This food-borne disease has killed 61 people in South Africa in the past year. It’s the worst documented outbreak in global history.

Juno: Listeriosis is the name of the disease. Listeria is the name of the bacterium that causes the disease.

V/O Dr Juno Thomas is Head of the Centre for Enteric Diseases at the National Institute for Com/muni/cable Diseases.

Juno: We find it in water, in soil, in vegetation and also some animals carry it in their guts and it's excreted in their faeces. But people only get ill and develop the disease that's called Listeriosis if they eat food that has become contaminated with the bacteria.

V/O: Rupert Thorp became ill on Boxing Day. It started with a fever, and vomiting, but he ignored the symptoms, hoping they’d go away.

Rupert: Then it became more severe, the fever started to escalate, more stomach cramps, nauseous, struggling to keep anything down.

Devi: Joint pain?

Rupert: At that stage, the joint pain I had, neck stiffness, all of that. I wasn’t sure if it was because I’d been lying on the couch for two days, or...

V/O: Eventually, on New Year’s Eve, Rupert went to see his GP and was diagnosed with Listeriosis and put on a drip.

Rupert: He didn’t do any blood tests, so he just said there is a bit of an outbreak, so it might be that.

Devi: But his diagnosis was listeriosis?

Rupet: Correct.

V/O: He was given an antibiotic and sent home to rest. Because no blood tests were done, he is not included in the 727 cases reported in the last year.

Link: Last week the Minister of Health declared Listeriosis a notifiable disease, which means doctors are legally compelled to report any cases to government officials. But before that, not all cases were reported, which means that the figures could be much higher.

V/O: What’s more, we don’t know what happened to all 727 cases that were reported, because only 134 patients have been followed up.

Juno: So, of the 134 patients that we can confirm what their final outcome was, there have been 61 deaths. I expect that the more data we get about patients who have been followed up, and we have final outcome details for those, our death numbers will increase.

V/O: So how does this killer bug get into our food? The bacteria can enter the food chain at any point between the farm and the fork.
Listeria can contaminate meat and meat products, dairy and dairy products, fresh fruit and vegetables and ready-to-eat meals.

Lucia: The deli meats, the cold cuts... quite a number of outbreaks have occurred due to those.

V/O: Dr Lucia Anelich is an international food safety expert.

Lucia: Soft cheeses that are made from unpasteurized milk have been implicated. Raw sprouts, pre-packaged salads. Meat pates, meat spreads, cold smoked fish. So, there are quite a number of products that have been implicated in other outbreaks internationally.

Devi: Schools open on Wednesday, busy parents do tend to use cold cuts, viennas to fill lunch boxes.

Lucia: If it cannot be cooked it should preferably, just simply be avoided.

Devi: When you are pregnant they tell you no sushi, no raw eggs, no soft cheese…?

Lucia: A pregnant woman can transfer the organism via her placenta to the unborn child, and that is the big risk.

Link: You might think that Listeriosis is like food poisoning, but it’s much worse. The mortality rate is 25% that’s 1 in 4 people – much higher than typhoid or bubonic plague.

V/O: 34-year-old Sonette Clack was pregnant with her third child in November last year. At 11-weeks she went to Steve Biko Hospital in Pretoria, and was told there was no heartbeat.

Tanja: When the baby died, when she had the miscarriage, they didn’t even do any tests on her or the baby to see what was the cause of the miscarriage.

V/O: Three weeks later, Tanja rushed to Steve Biko when her daughter was admitted to casualty unconscious. Sonette was diagnosed with meningitis, and after 5 days was on life support in ICU. The doctors said she was brain dead.

Tanja: So, we were very heart sore and broken, because we couldn’t believe that this is the end. Although I know that from that Wednesday she was already dead, but it’s just for me to go there and feel she is still warm, and feel her heart beat. For me it was like she was still alive. But then we decide to put down the machines the Saturday morning. So, they put down the machines Saturday morning, the 9th at 11:30.

V/O: Sonette had Listeriosis, which caused the miscarriage and the meningitis. But with an incubation period of up to 70 days, it’s almost impossible to say where she got it.

Tanja: While she was pregnant she had a craving for fruit, They had polony, not most of the time, but they had that a lot. They also had poultry, chicken and mince they had a lot.

Juno: But to date we haven’t been able to hone in on a specific food that all of those patients seem to eat.

V/O; But intensive DNA testing has narrowed the search, by identifying the particular strain of Listeria that has caused the outbreak.

Juno: All our human cases that we’ve done this whole genome sequencing on to date, 91% of them belong to a single strain, and that’s our outbreak strain.

Lucia: The fact that it’s ST6 in 91% of the cases, actually means that it probably comes from a single source, a single processing environment. It could be one food processed in that processing environment, or multiple food products processed in that single processing environment.

V/O: While most cases are in Gauteng, the outbreak has been recorded nationwide, in both public and private hospitals.


Link; The source is probably a food product – widely distributed and consumed across all socioeconomic groups. But until it’s found, we are all at risk.
